summary: Voters at the March 7, 2026 Special Town Meeting adopted Article 4, a zoning moratorium on large-scale ground-mounted solar and battery storage through Sep 30, 2026. The Attorney General disapproved it on June 22, 2026, citing G.L. c. 40A, § 3.

H.5641 (Rep. Leigh Davis, Sen. Paul Mark), approved by Becket voters as Article 5 on March 7, 2026, would authorize a six-month moratorium on large-scale solar and battery storage, exempting residential batteries. It was referred to the Joint Committee on Municipalities and Regional Government on Aug 4, 2026, with a written-testimony hearing set for Sep 21, 2026.

The Feb 24, 2026 Special Town Meeting passed three zoning moratoriums (Articles 6 to 8): a town-wide pause on large ground-mounted solar and storage over 600 kWh through June 30, 2027, plus limited-area moratoriums on solar and on energy storage. The Attorney General disapproved all three in a June 8, 2026 letter.

H.5294 (Rep. Lindsay Sabadosa, Sen. Paul Mark), approved by Worthington voters as Article 10 on Feb 24, 2026, sought a one-year moratorium on large ground-mounted solar and battery storage. The Municipalities committee sent it to a study order (H.5480) on June 8, 2026, a committee action rather than a floor vote that usually ends a bill for the session.

Annual Town Meeting voters in May 2026 approved a moratorium on commercial battery energy storage systems through Nov 14, 2026. The Attorney General disapproved it on Aug 31, 2026 for lacking justification and conflicting with the consolidated-permit requirement that began Oct 1, 2026.

On Oct 1, 2026, Special Town Meeting voters unanimously approved Article 4, a new Clean Energy zoning section with revised solar and wind rules and the town's first battery storage rules, based largely on the state energy department’s model framework. As a town zoning bylaw it is subject to Attorney General review.

The April 27, 2026 Special Town Meeting passed Article 63 (118 to 13), a moratorium on standalone battery storage of 250 kWh or more through Dec 1, 2026. The Attorney General disapproved it on Aug 13, 2026 as unjustified, unlimited in scope and in conflict with the consolidated-permit requirement.

Sutton said it would begin accepting consolidated local permit applications for small clean-energy facilities, including solar and battery storage, on Oct 1, 2026, with the Town Manager serving as Local Government Representative. As of its July 2, 2026 notice the town had not decided whether to adopt a local permitting bylaw or rely on the state energy department’s model rules.

The Nov 17, 2025 Special Town Meeting adopted Article 1, a moratorium on large-scale ground-mounted solar and battery storage through May 31, 2026. The Attorney General disapproved it on March 11, 2026 (Case #12153), finding no articulated health, safety or welfare justification.

The May 6, 2024 Annual Town Meeting adopted a moratorium on principal-use battery storage (Article 26) and one on large-scale ground-mounted solar including agrivoltaics (Article 27), both running to August 2025. The Attorney General disapproved both moratoriums on Oct 30, 2024 (Case #11346) but approved a new battery storage definition.

A May 1, 2024 Special Town Meeting adopted a general bylaw to license battery energy storage systems; the Attorney General disapproved it on Nov 14, 2024, ruling it regulated land use and had to be adopted as a zoning bylaw. The town sued, and the Land Court upheld the disapproval on Mar 12, 2026 (Town of Wendell v. Campbell, 25 MISC 000014) affirmed the disapproval.

Article 32 of the June 3, 2024 Annual Town Meeting amended the zoning bylaw to regulate battery energy storage systems. The Attorney General approved it on Sep 5, 2024 (Case #11474), finding it consistent with the solar protections of G.L. c. 40A, § 3.

Article 23 of the May 2, 2024 Annual Town Meeting added energy storage definitions and a new Large Energy Storage Systems section to the zoning bylaw. The Attorney General approved it on Nov 12, 2024 (Case #11355), except a ban on earth removal to facilitate a storage installation, which was disapproved.

Articles 3 to 8 of the Dec 8, 2025 Special Town Meeting revised the town's solar and battery storage zoning. The Attorney General approved them on Aug 13, 2026 (Case #12175), except a rule barring battery storage from being visible from public roads and a requirement that owners pay for emergency-responder equipment and training.

Zoning ordinance Section 5-31 (dated Feb 26, 2026) made battery energy storage systems a prohibited use in all districts as an interim restriction, covering standalone systems and accessory systems of 250 kWh or more. By its terms it ran through Sep 30, 2026 or until superseding zoning is adopted; no extension had been found as of Oct 10, 2026, so it appears to have lapsed.

The City Council voted 8 to 0 to pause new battery storage site development, alongside a data center moratorium, effective until July 31, 2027. Two battery projects already underway, on Lancaster Street and Willard Street, are not paused.

Council President Frank Laflamme proposed a zoning ordinance amendment to define and regulate battery energy storage, first discussed Aug 4, 2026 and referred to the Planning Department and the Zoning and Ordinance subcommittees. As of the Sep 15, 2026 council meeting it still had steps remaining before returning to the full council.

Town Meeting adopted a six-month moratorium on standalone battery storage permits (Article 18, Nov 2024 Special Town Meeting). The Attorney General disapproved it on Mar 11, 2025; the town later adopted battery-storage zoning that the Attorney General approved on Feb 9, 2026.

Annual Town Meeting voters in June 2026 passed Article 24, a standalone battery storage zoning section based on the state energy department’s model bylaw that bans mid- and large-scale systems in the Aquifer Protection District and within 300 feet of drinking-water or agricultural wells. It follows a Nov 12, 2025 amendment capping battery storage at 250 kWh in the aquifer district.

A Planning Board draft would replace Harvard's large-scale solar overlay district with a town-wide Clean Energy Facilities bylaw that regulates battery storage for the first time and adds a consolidated local permit option. The first Planning Board hearing was scheduled for Aug 17, 2026.

A proposed Article 18 zoning bylaw would set standards for solar and battery storage and add a consolidated local permitting section aligned with 225 CMR 29.00. A Sep 10, 2026 draft shows the Town Council's Community Resources Committee recommended it after first reading.

The Planning Board proposed a temporary moratorium on special permit applications for solar arrays and battery storage (Article 3), but at the Nov 12, 2025 Special Town Meeting the Select Board took no action and no vote was held. A Select Board member said the article would not have been legally binding.

The Planning Board began drafting battery storage zoning rules on Jan 7, 2026, working from the state energy department’s draft model bylaw with help from the Pioneer Valley Planning Commission. A Town Meeting vote was not found.

A Dec 30, 2025 draft battery storage zoning amendment prepared for the March 2026 Annual Town Meeting would allow battery storage by special permit in certain business and planned-development districts and prohibit them in roughly 90% of town. The Town Meeting outcome was not found.

The Oct 6, 2026 City Council agenda lists a Planning Board request to amend Chapter 181 of the zoning code to set a temporary zoning moratorium on locally regulated commercial battery storage. From the city’s posted agenda.

Materials for the Oct 13, 2026 City Council meeting report that the Ordinances and Rules Committee voted 5–0 to recommend approving a proposed Battery Energy Storage Systems zoning amendment, as amended. From the city’s posted agenda.

The Select Board's Oct 13, 2026 agenda includes reviewing a warrant article to create zoning Section 6.6 for Small Clean Energy Infrastructure Facilities, the category covered by the state's new consolidated permit. From the town’s posted agenda.

A package of zoning and code amendments to adopt consolidated local permitting standards for Small Clean Energy Infrastructure Facilities under 225 CMR 29.00 was scheduled for an Oct 8, 2026 joint hearing of the Planning Board and the council's Legislative Matters Committee. From the city’s posted agenda.
A Battery Energy Storage System bylaw is on the Planning Board's Oct 14, 2026 agenda. From the town’s posted agenda.

Hanson's battery storage article imposed a two-year town-wide moratorium on Tier 1 battery storage and allowed Tier 2 only in an overlay district that was never mapped. The Attorney General disapproved the whole article. (Article 34 (May 1, 2023 Annual Town Meeting).)

Southwick adopted a moratorium on large solar and battery storage through May 31, 2027. The Attorney General disapproved it for lacking any health, safety or welfare justification and for procedural defects. (Article 5 (Jan 13, 2026 Special Town Meeting).)

Chesterfield adopted a battery storage moratorium through Sep 30, 2026. The Attorney General disapproved it for lacking any health, safety or welfare justification. (Article 3 (June 24, 2026 Special Town Meeting).)

Gill's Article 7 imposed a moratorium on battery storage and data centers until May 3, 2027. The Attorney General disapproved the battery storage part but approved the data-center part, since data centers are not a protected use. (Article 7 (May 4, 2026 Annual Town Meeting).)

Brookfield prohibited all battery storage in every district through Nov 30, 2026. The Attorney General disapproved it for lacking justification, for unlawful scope, for conflicting with the consolidated permit law, and for procedural defects. (Article 35 (June 4, 2026 Annual Town Meeting).)
